result:
Your teammate's "it's a tiny diff" framing is exactly the trap here — line count doesn't track risk. This PR bundles a prompt change, a new autonomous money-moving tool, and a public trust claim being deleted. Each is a controlled item on its own, and together they represent a policy decision (bot can now issue refunds without a human) that a smoke test won't surface.

| Item | Type | Current state | Intended state | Why controlled | Evidence / gap | Owner | Re-check trigger |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Support-bot system prompt | Prompt | Existing wording (baseline before PR) | New "more proactive" wording | Directly shapes agent behavior toward customers; "proactive" language can push the bot toward taking more unilateral action, which interacts directly with item #2 | PR diff (link it) — no gap if diff is the record | Bot's prompt owner / eng lead | Any future prompt edit, or if support logs show the bot acting more aggressively/overstepping than expected |
| `issue_refund(amount, order_id)` tool + $50 autonomy threshold | Tool / agent-power grant | No refund tool exists; all refunds require human sign-off | Agent can autonomously approve refunds up to $50, no human in the loop | This is a grant of financial authority to an autonomous agent — the single highest-risk item in the PR | **Gap**: no sign-off evident from finance, risk, or security on granting autonomous spend authority — engineering review ≠ business approval | Should be co-owned by eng lead + a finance/risk owner (name one before merge) | Any change to the $ threshold, any refund-abuse incident, or first N days of production usage (should have a monitoring/rollback plan, not just a smoke test) |
| Help-center article: "A human always reviews refunds before they are issued." | Public claim / doc | Sentence present, stating human-in-the-loop guarantee | Sentence deleted | This is a public-facing trust claim. Deleting it quietly, in the same PR that removes the human review it describes, changes what customers are told about the system — that's a comms/policy decision, not a code cleanup | **Gap**: no evidence of support/legal/comms sign-off on removing this guarantee; deleting the sentence doesn't equal deciding it's OK to no longer make that promise | Support content owner + legal/comms (name one before merge) | Any future change to refund policy, or if a customer/support escalation references the old promise |

**What this means for merging:** items 2 and 3 are not independent of each other — you're simultaneously granting the bot money authority and erasing the public statement that contradicted it. That's a policy change wearing a code-PR costume. A smoke test verifies the tool *works*; it doesn't verify anyone with authority over refund policy or public claims *approved* the change.

Before merging, I'd get an explicit owner and yes/no from whoever owns refund policy (finance/risk) and whoever owns the help-center content (support/legal), even if it's a quick Slack sign-off — not because the code is risky, but because the decision to let a bot move money unsupervised and stop telling customers a human checks it isn't an engineering call alone.
